opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing I'd most like to see is better hands. So much of what makes humans useful in the physical world comes down to dexterity, and most robots today are still using parallel-jaw grippers or fairly crude multi-fingered hands. They're fine for pick-and-place, but the moment you want a robot to fold laundry properly, manipulate a tool, or handle something deformable or fragile, you hit a wall. A robust, affordable, dexterous hand that doesn't break after a few thousand hours of operation would unlock a huge amount of capability, especially now that the learning side is getting good enough to actually use that dexterity.

Closely tied to that is touch. Vision has carried us a long way, but humans rely heavily on tactile feedback, like feeling slip, sensing how hard you're squeezing, knowing when you've made contact. Good tactile skins that are high-resolution, durable, and cheap enough to cover a whole hand or arm would give our models a much richer signal to learn from. Right now a lot of tactile sensors are either research prototypes or wear out quickly.

Beyond that, I'd say reliability and cost in general. A lot of robot learning is bottlenecked on data, and data collection is bottlenecked on how many robots you can run, how often they break, and how much it costs to fix them. If hardware became cheap and robust enough that you could deploy fleets of them in real homes and workplaces, the data flywheel would spin much faster. That matters more to me than any single flashy capability.

And finally, safety and compliance. If robots are going to work alongside people, they need to be inherently safe, lighter, with compliant actuators and backdrivable joints, so that a mistake by the policy doesn't turn into someone getting hurt. That's something hardware can solve in ways that software alone can't guarantee.

So if I had to rank them: dexterous hands, tactile sensing, then cheap and reliable platforms that let us scale data. Those are the things I think would most accelerate the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that hardware is still the bottleneck in a way that software people sometimes underestimate. When we were doing the RT-1 and RT-2 work at Google, the learning side moved incredibly fast, but the robots themselves were the same platforms for years, and every limitation of the body shows up as a limitation of the policy.

The first thing I'd want is better hands. Most research robots still have a parallel-jaw gripper, which is basically a pair of tweezers. You can do a surprising amount with that, but a huge fraction of real tasks need in-hand manipulation, compliance, and some sense of touch. Dexterous hands exist, but they tend to be fragile, expensive, and hard to maintain, and they break right when you're in the middle of a data collection run. I'd love a hand that is cheap enough to treat as a consumable and robust enough to survive a few thousand hours of learned, slightly clumsy behavior.

Closely tied to that is tactile sensing. Vision gets you far, but the moment you're grasping something soft or occluded, you're flying blind. Dense, durable tactile skin that doesn't drift and doesn't need recalibration every week would change what policies can learn. Right now a lot of us are substituting force feedback from motor currents, which is a poor proxy.

The second big one is reliability and repairability. Learning-based robotics is fundamentally a data game. If you want tens of thousands of episodes, you need fleets of robots running for weeks with minimal babysitting. Things like actuators that don't overheat, cables that don't fray, and a design where a grad student can swap a part in fifteen minutes instead of shipping the arm back to the vendor. That's unglamorous, but it probably matters more for progress than any single clever mechanism.

Third, I'd push for safe, compliant actuation. Collaborative arms are a good start, but I'd like robots that can be bumped into, that can bump into things, and that fail gracefully. When the robot is inherently safe, you can let the policy explore more, collect data in messier environments, and put humans in the loop without a cage. That unlocks a lot of the learning approaches that look good on paper but are scary to run on stiff industrial hardware.

And then there's cost. The real inflection point for learning in language and vision was that data became abundant and cheap. In robotics, every data point costs real money in hardware, space, and human time. If someone can drive a capable mobile manipulator down to the price of a decent laptop, the whole field changes, because suddenly you can have hundreds of them instead of five.

If I had to pick one, I'd say the hands plus touch. A good body with poor hands caps what you can do, whereas great hands on a mediocre arm still let you learn a lot. But all of these are really in service of the same goal, which is making robots cheap and durable enough that we can throw learning at them at scale.

astra-6.text:
I’d really like to see hardware become more reliable, more affordable, and easier to collect data on. From the learning side, you want robots that can run for long periods, doing lots of different tasks, without needing someone to constantly repair or recalibrate them. That makes a huge difference to how quickly you can iterate.

Dexterous hands and tactile sensing would also be high on my list. There’s so much information in contact that vision alone doesn’t give you. If you’re holding something, is it slipping? Are you applying too much force? Can you adjust your grasp without putting it down and starting over? Having reliable sensing and actuation for those interactions would open up a much richer set of tasks.

And I’d love for those capabilities to be accessible to more researchers. A really capable robot is exciting, but a robot that lots of people can afford and operate reliably could have an even bigger impact on progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d love to see hardware that lets us collect a lot more experience reliably. As a learning researcher, you want the robot to keep running, so you can focus on improving the policy instead of constantly repairing the platform or recalibrating sensors.

Dexterous hands are also a big one. There’s so much in everyday life that becomes possible when you have a reliable hand, good tactile sensing, and enough compliance to interact with objects safely. You can get surprisingly far with a parallel-jaw gripper, but it constrains the tasks you can learn.

And then cost. If we can make capable robots cheaper and easier to maintain, we can have more of them collecting data in more varied environments. I think that combination—reliability, dexterity, and affordability—would be really powerful for learning.
